missions/china-inland-mission/name: China Inland Mission (Hudson Taylor, 1865) and the faith-mission model
missions/china-inland-mission/origin/nam: Brighton, England (founding prayer, June 1865); London headquarters
missions/china-inland-mission/statusNote: Forced out of China by the Communist government between 1950 and 1953, the CIM moved its headquarters to Singapore, redeployed to East and Southeast Asia and became the Overseas Missionary Fellowship (1964), now OMF International. It remains active, and since the 1980s has again engaged with Chinese Christians, though not as a mission inside the People's Republic.
missions/china-inland-mission/summary: The pioneer 'faith mission', founded by James Hudson Taylor in 1865 to evangelise China's unreached inland provinces. Interdenominational, directed from China rather than from home, without guaranteed salaries or public appeals for money, and willing to send working-class men and single women inland in Chinese dress, it became the largest Protestant mission in China, suffered grievously in the Boxer rising of 1900, and was the model for dozens of later faith missions worldwide.
missions/china-inland-mission/story:
Hudson Taylor (1832–1905), a Methodist-raised chemist's son from Barnsley, went to China in 1853–54 with the small Chinese Evangelisation Society, which proved unreliable in supporting him. Influenced by George Müller of Bristol and the Brethren ideal of 'living by faith', he resigned, adopted Chinese dress and the queue, married Maria Dyer in Ningbo (1858), and returned to England in 1860 in broken health. While revising the Ningbo romanised New Testament he became haunted by China's interior, where eleven provinces had no Protestant missionary. On Brighton beach on 25 June 1865 he prayed for 'twenty-four willing, skilful labourers', opened a bank account in the name of the China Inland Mission two days later, and in October published China's Spiritual Need and Claims, with its refrain that 'a million a month' were dying in China without Christ.

The CIM's principles defined the faith-mission model. Missionaries of any evangelical denomination were accepted if they held the mission's conservative doctrinal basis; no salaries were guaranteed and no debts incurred; there were no public collections or appeals — needs were made known to God in prayer; leadership was exercised in China by a director on the field, not by a committee at home; missionaries were to wear Chinese dress, live simply and press inland; and candidates without university or theological education, including artisans and single women, were welcome. In May 1866 Taylor sailed on the Lammermuir with a party of sixteen recruits, reaching Shanghai in September and settling in Hangzhou. The party's Chinese dress and working-class origins provoked scorn from other missionaries, and internal quarrels soon tested Taylor's authority.

Expansion was steady and costly. In 1868 a riot at Yangzhou wounded the Taylors and their colleagues; British consular use of gunboats in response, which Taylor had not requested, brought censure in Parliament. Maria Taylor died in 1870. In 1875 Taylor appealed for eighteen men for the nine unreached provinces, and by the early 1880s CIM itinerants had travelled through nearly all of them; from the 1880s single women were stationed inland, an unprecedented step. The 'Cambridge Seven' (1885), including the cricketer C. T. Studd, brought the mission celebrity and helped inspire the student volunteer movements; appeals for 'the Seventy' (1881), 'the Hundred' (1887) and 1,000 new workers for China (1890) were met. Taylor's Keswick-style 'exchanged life' spirituality and his insistence on simplicity made the CIM a symbol of evangelical devotion. By 1900 it was the largest Protestant mission in China, with roughly 750–800 missionaries.

The Boxer rising of 1900 was the mission's darkest hour. The Boxers (Yihequan), a movement of young peasants in drought-stricken Shandong and Zhili, attacked foreigners and Chinese Christians as the source of China's humiliation; in June 1900 the Qing court declared war on the foreign powers. In Shanxi the governor Yuxian had 44 foreigners, including Protestant missionary families and Catholic bishops and nuns, executed at Taiyuan on 9 July. In all some 188 Protestant missionaries and children were killed, together with tens of thousands of Chinese Christians (about 30,000 Catholics and some 2,000 Protestants). The CIM lost 58 missionaries and 21 children, more than any other society. Taylor, then elderly and ill in Switzerland, and his successor Dixon Hoste refused to claim compensation for the mission's losses — an act contrasted sharply with the punitive indemnities sought by others. Taylor died in Changsha, Hunan, in 1905.

Under Hoste (1902–35) the CIM continued to grow, reaching about 1,300 missionaries in the mid-1930s after a 1929 appeal for 'the Two Hundred'. It developed work among minority peoples — James O. Fraser among the Lisu of Yunnan, with a script devised with the Karen evangelist Ba Thaw, and others among the Nosu, Miao and Tibetans — and its Chinese leaders and partners, such as the Shanxi scholar-evangelist Xi Shengmo ('Pastor Hsi'), built churches that survived without missionaries. It withdrew from the National Christian Council of China in 1926 over theological liberalism. Civil war brought danger: John and Betty Stam were beheaded by Communist soldiers in Anhui in 1934, and Rudolf Bosshardt was held by the Red Army on the Long March.

After the Communist victory of 1949 the CIM at first resolved to stay. But the Korean War, the 'Three-Self' Christian Manifesto of 1950 and denunciation campaigns that branded missionaries as agents of imperialism made their presence a danger to Chinese Christians. In January 1951 the directors ordered a complete withdrawal — the 'reluctant exodus'. Over the next two years several hundred missionaries and their children left, the last few, including Arthur and Wilda Mathews, only in 1953. Meeting in Bournemouth in 1951 the leaders resolved to redeploy to the Chinese diaspora and to other unreached peoples of East Asia, with a new headquarters in Singapore. As the Overseas Missionary Fellowship (from 1964) it works in Thailand, Japan, the Philippines, Indonesia, Taiwan, Malaysia and elsewhere, and accepts Asian missionaries as full members. Meanwhile the Chinese churches the CIM helped to plant, deprived of foreign aid, grew under persecution into one of the largest Protestant populations in the world.
missions/china-inland-mission/beliefs/0: Conservative evangelical doctrine: the divine inspiration and authority of Scripture, the Trinity, the fall, substitutionary atonement, justification by faith, bodily resurrection and the eternal punishment of the lost.
missions/china-inland-mission/beliefs/1: Urgency driven by the conviction that millions were perishing without having heard the gospel ('a million a month in China are dying without God').
missions/china-inland-mission/beliefs/2: The 'faith principle': God's work done in God's way will not lack God's supply — no guaranteed salaries, no debt and no public solicitation of funds, following George Müller.
missions/china-inland-mission/beliefs/3: Premillennial expectation of Christ's return, which gave priority to proclaiming the gospel widely rather than building Christian civilisation.
missions/china-inland-mission/beliefs/4: Keswick-style holiness spirituality — rest in Christ, the 'exchanged life' and total consecration — as the inner life of mission.
missions/china-inland-mission/beliefs/5: Interdenominational evangelical unity: Anglicans, Baptists, Presbyterians, Methodists and Brethren served together, with churches organised according to the missionaries' convictions in each district.
missions/china-inland-mission/strategies: Direction from the field: authority lay with the General Director and China Council in Shanghai rather than with a home committee.
Pioneering itineration to all the inland provinces, followed by the establishment of permanent stations and outstations.
Identification with the Chinese through Chinese dress, diet and housing, and residence in interior towns rather than treaty ports.
Recruitment of lay men and women without formal theological training, including single women sent inland as evangelists from the 1880s.
Prayer-based appeals for specific numbers of workers (the Eighteen, the Seventy, the Hundred, the Two Hundred) publicised through the magazine China's Millions.
Opium refuges and simple medical work, combined with outspoken opposition to the British opium trade.
Work among non-Han peoples (Lisu, Nosu, Miao, Tibetans) using indigenous scripts and local evangelists.
missions/china-inland-mission/groupsReac: Han Chinese in the inland provinces — Zhejiang, Jiangxi, Anhui, Henan, Shanxi, Shaanxi, Gansu, Sichuan, Guizhou, Yunnan and Hunan.
The Lisu, Lahu and other peoples of western Yunnan, where large people movements took place.
The Nosu (Yi) and A-Hmao (Miao) of Guizhou and Yunnan, and Tibetans on the western borders.
Hui Muslims of the north-west, among whom the CIM attempted specialised work with little numerical result.
Opium addicts, rural women and the poor through refuges, girls' schools and itinerant evangelism.
After 1951, Chinese diaspora communities and tribal peoples of Thailand, Malaysia, Indonesia and the Philippines, and the Japanese.
missions/china-inland-mission/challenges: Riots and anti-foreign violence, from Yangzhou (1868) to the Boxer rising, in which the CIM lost 58 missionaries and 21 children.
Financial uncertainty inherent in the faith principle, with periods of severe shortage.
Internal conflict over Taylor's authority, especially in the Lammermuir party and in tensions with the London council in the 1880s–90s.
Disease, isolation and high death rates among missionaries and their children inland.
Civil war, banditry and Communist hostility in the 1920s–40s, including the murder of John and Betty Stam (1934).
The 1950–53 accusation campaigns that turned association with foreign missionaries into a liability for Chinese Christians, forcing total withdrawal.
missions/china-inland-mission/harms/0: Although Taylor disliked gunboat diplomacy, the mission's inland presence depended on the unequal treaties and extraterritorial rights imposed on China by Western powers.
missions/china-inland-mission/harms/1: Missionary rhetoric depicted Chinese religion and culture as darkness and idolatry, feeding Chinese perceptions of missions as cultural aggression.
missions/china-inland-mission/harms/2: Leadership remained in foreign hands for decades; devolution to Chinese leaders was slow and partial compared with the mission's own ideals.
missions/china-inland-mission/harms/3: Christian converts' disputes with neighbours, sometimes backed by missionary intervention, contributed to local resentments that the Boxers exploited.
missions/china-inland-mission/harms/4: Separatist theology encouraged withdrawal from social and political questions and suspicion of Chinese Christians who engaged with nationalism.
missions/china-inland-mission/harms/5: The faith principle could mask hardship, leaving missionaries and their families in poverty and ill health.
missions/china-inland-mission/developmen: Created the faith-mission model — interdenominational, field-directed, lay and women-inclusive — copied by dozens of missions worldwide.
Opened Protestant work in almost every inland province of China and among many minority peoples.
Gave single women unprecedented responsibility as evangelists and station leaders.
Fraser's Lisu script and Bible and other minority-language work remain foundations of churches in Yunnan and Myanmar.
Refusal of Boxer compensation became a widely cited example of non-retaliation in mission.
Chinese churches it helped plant survived missionary withdrawal and grew under persecution; OMF continues as an international, increasingly Asian mission.
missions/china-inland-mission/outcome: The CIM grew from Taylor's 1865 prayer into the largest Protestant mission in China, then withdrew completely in 1951–53. It reinvented itself as the Overseas Missionary Fellowship (OMF International), while its greatest legacy — Chinese churches able to survive without foreigners and the faith-mission model itself — outlasted its presence in China.

missions/china-inland-mission/journeys/0: Hudson Taylor's first voyage to China (1853–54)
Taylor sailed from Liverpool on the Dumfries in September 1853 for the Chinese Evangelisation Society and landed at Shanghai, then in the midst of the Small Swords occupation, on 1 March 1854.
missions/china-inland-mission/journeys/1: Hudson and Maria Taylor, their children and sixteen recruits
The Lammermuir left London on 26 May 1866, survived two typhoons in the China Sea and reached Shanghai on 30 September; the party moved up the canals to Hangzhou in November, adopting Chinese dress.
missions/china-inland-mission/journeys/2: C. T. Studd, Stanley Smith, Montagu Beauchamp, Dixon Hoste, William Cassels and Arthur and Cecil Polhill-Turner
After farewell meetings that stirred British universities, the seven sailed in February 1885 and dispersed inland, some to Shanxi and others to Shaanxi and Sichuan.
missions/china-inland-mission/journeys/3: Missionaries in the interior obtained exit permits, often after months of delay, travelled to the coast and crossed the border at Lo Wu into Hong Kong; the mission's leaders regrouped in Singapore and redeployed workers to Thailand, Malaya, Japan and beyond.
missions/china-inland-mission/relations/: The CIM's principles were explicitly copied by the Sudan Interior Mission, Africa Inland Mission, Sudan United Mission, WEC and others, often founded by people with CIM links.
The Cambridge Seven (1885) inspired the student mission movement; the CIM drew many recruits from the British and North American student volunteers.
After the CIM's withdrawal in 1951–53, the churches it helped to plant continued under Chinese leadership, some in the Three-Self churches and many in independent house churches.
Its focus on unreached inland regions anticipated the post-war evangelical emphasis on 'unreached peoples'.
missions/china-inland-mission/agreements: Shared the faith principle, interdenominational evangelical basis, lay recruitment and focus on unreached interiors.
Taylor's adoption of Chinese dress and residence echoed, in a Protestant key, the Jesuit practice of cultural identification pioneered by Ricci — though without accommodation of Chinese rites.
Shared a priority on vernacular scriptures, including minority-language Bibles in Lisu and Miao.
missions/china-inland-mission/disagreeme: Represented the faith-mission alternative to denominational boards: no guaranteed salaries, no public appeals, direction from the field and acceptance of non-ordained and less-educated missionaries.

Withdrew from the National Christian Council of China in 1926 and kept aloof from ecumenical bodies, rejecting the theological liberalism of the Laymen's Inquiry (1932) and later the World Council of Churches.
Gave priority to widespread evangelism over the large institutional programmes (universities, hospitals) favoured by the denominational boards.
missions/china-inland-mission/deviations: A mission dedicated to identification with the Chinese nonetheless kept leadership in Western hands until after it left China.
Founded to evangelise and then move on, the CIM in practice built long-term stations, schools (such as the Chefoo School for missionaries' children) and institutions.
The no-solicitation principle coexisted with highly effective publicity through China's Millions and well-publicised appeals for workers.
